content:
NHS physiotherapy is free but there may be a long waiting list. While you wait for community or home-visit physio, you can usually start safe, gentle exercise yourself, keep moving little and often, and use your pain relief as agreed with your GP or pharmacist. Check whether your area lets you refer yourself to the NHS musculoskeletal (MSK) service, ask about telephone, video or group sessions, and ask whether a physiotherapist can visit you at home if you cannot get out. Contact the service or your GP if you are getting worse, falling, or can no longer manage at home, as they may be able to review your priority. Get urgent help for a hot, swollen joint with fever, new weakness or numbness, or loss of bladder or bowel control. Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself.

This guide is about the wait itself when getting out is hard. For how NHS physiotherapy referral and self-referral work in general, see getting arthritis physiotherapy on the NHS. For what a home visit involves, see home-visit physiotherapy.

First, make sure you are on the right list

  • Check you have been referred. If you have heard nothing, phone the service or your GP surgery to check the referral arrived and ask roughly how long the wait is.
  • Ask about self-referral. The NHS says that in many areas you can go straight to the community MSK service without a GP referral. Your GP surgery may also have a first contact physiotherapist who can assess you sooner.
  • Tell them what makes getting there hard. If you cannot get to a clinic, ask whether a physiotherapist can see you at home, or by phone or video.
  • Ask about classes. Some areas run group sessions for joint pain, such as ESCAPE-pain for knee and hip pain, and strength and balance classes through the falls service. These sometimes start sooner than one-to-one appointments.

Safe things you can start now

NICE (NG226) says exercise and advice are core treatments for osteoarthritis, so you do not need to wait for permission to start gently. The aim is to keep joints moving and muscles working, not to push through sharp pain.

  • Move little and often. Get up and move around every hour or so in the day, even for a minute or two.
  • Practise standing up from a chair a few times, slowly, using your arms if you need to. See sit-to-stand practice.
  • Do seated strength exercises such as knee straightening and ankle pumps. See seated strength exercises.
  • Keep your balance working by standing at the kitchen worktop and holding on while you do simple balance moves. The NHS older adults guidelines recommend activities that improve strength and balance on at least two days a week.
  • Use pain relief as agreed with your GP or pharmacist so you can move, and heat or cold if it helps. See pain relief options.

Some ache during and after exercise is normal and usually settles within a day. If pain is much worse the next day, do less next time rather than stopping altogether.

Write down what physio needs to know

Use the wait to note down a few things, so your first appointment is spent on treatment rather than history:

  • which joints hurt, and what makes them better or worse
  • the everyday tasks you find hardest, such as stairs, getting out of bed, the bath or the toilet
  • any falls or near misses
  • your medicines, and what you have tried so far
  • what you most want to get back to doing

When to chase or ask for an earlier appointment

Contact the physio service or your GP if, while you wait:

  • you have had a fall, or you are nearly falling more often
  • you can no longer manage stairs, washing, dressing or getting to the toilet
  • you are spending most of the day in a chair or bed
  • pain is much worse, keeps you awake every night, or painkillers are no longer helping

Services can sometimes change your priority when things get worse, but only if they know. If daily tasks at home are getting too hard, you can also ask your council for a free care needs assessment, which can lead to equipment and help from an occupational therapist.

When not to wait

  • Get same-day help (urgent GP appointment or NHS 111) for a joint that is suddenly hot, swollen and very painful, especially with a temperature.
  • Call 999 or go to A&E if you have back pain with numbness around your bottom or genitals, or new problems controlling your bladder or bowels, or if you have sudden weakness in your legs.
  • Call 999 after a fall if you may have hurt your head, neck, back or hip, or cannot get up.

If you are not sure whether it is a flare or something else, see is it a flare or something else.

For family and carers

You can help by checking the referral has arrived, writing down the notes above, and keeping an eye on whether the person is doing less over time. Doing the exercises together can help with motivation, and you can call the service on their behalf if they agree.

Common questions

Can I pay for private physio while I wait?

Yes, if you choose to. The NHS advises choosing a physiotherapist who is chartered (MCSP) and registered with the Health and Care Professions Council (HCPC). Ask whether they do home visits and what it will cost before you book.

Will exercising before I see the physio make my arthritis worse?

Gentle, regular exercise is very unlikely to harm arthritic joints and usually helps. Start small and build up slowly. Stop and get advice if a joint becomes hot and swollen.

What if I cannot get to group classes?

Tell the service. Ask about home visits, phone or video appointments, or a printed home exercise programme.
